reference.source: Williams Hematology / WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours
clinicalPearls: An indolent clonal proliferation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes that classically presents with neutropenia, often with recurrent bacterial infection or an incidental finding
The blood film shows an increase in large granular lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm containing azurophilic granules
A characteristic association exists with rheumatoid arthritis and with Felty-like syndrome (neutropenia and splenomegaly)
The typical immunophenotype is CD3, CD8 and CD57 positive with expression of cytotoxic markers, and clonality is confirmed by T-cell receptor gene rearrangement
Activating mutations in the STAT3 gene are found in a substantial proportion of cases and support the diagnosis
Many patients follow a chronic course and are observed; immunosuppression is reserved for symptomatic cytopenias or transfusion dependence
Anaemia, including a pure red cell aplasia pattern, and thrombocytopenia may accompany the neutropenia
reference.pathophysiology: T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukaemia arises from a clonal expansion of mature cytotoxic (usually CD8 positive) T lymphocytes. Chronic antigen-driven stimulation is thought to trigger the expansion, which then escapes normal apoptotic control through constitutive activation of the JAK/STAT signalling pathway, frequently driven by acquired activating mutations in STAT3. The persistent cytotoxic clone suppresses granulopoiesis and erythropoiesis in the marrow and, together with autoimmune mechanisms, produces the neutropenia, anaemia and thrombocytopenia that dominate the clinical picture. The strong link with rheumatoid arthritis reflects the shared background of dysregulated immune activation.
additionalDifferentials: Reactive large granular lymphocytosis from viral infection
Chronic lymphoproliferative disorder of NK cells
Felty syndrome without a demonstrable clone
Aplastic anaemia or hypoplastic myelodysplastic syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film review to quantify large granular lymphocytes
Flow cytometry immunophenotyping (CD3, CD8, CD57, CD16, cytotoxic markers)
T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies to demonstrate clonality
Molecular testing for STAT3 (and STAT5b) mutations
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to assess infiltration and cytopenia cause
Autoimmune serology including rheumatoid factor given the arthritis association
redFlags: Severe neutropenia with recurrent or life-threatening infection
Rapidly rising lymphocyte count or transformation to an aggressive phenotype
Constitutional symptoms suggesting an alternative aggressive lymphoproliferative disorder
reference.prognosis: Most patients have an indolent disease with prolonged survival, and morbidity relates mainly to infection from neutropenia; a minority have refractory cytopenias or, rarely, aggressive transformation.
pitfalls: Assuming a modest large granular lymphocytosis is reactive without checking clonality
Overlooking STAT3 mutation testing that can clarify a borderline diagnosis
Attributing neutropenia solely to rheumatoid arthritis or its drugs
Treating asymptomatic patients who could simply be monitored
management: Observe asymptomatic patients, as many follow an indolent course requiring no immediate treatment
Treat symptomatic cytopenias or transfusion dependence with immunosuppressive therapy such as methotrexate, ciclosporin or cyclophosphamide as first-line agents
Support the neutropenia with prompt treatment of infection, infection prophylaxis and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor when needed, and transfuse for symptomatic anaemia
Treat any associated rheumatoid arthritis or other autoimmune disease
Monitor blood counts for progression, refractory cytopenias or rare aggressive transformation
Refer to haematology and consider second-line or JAK/STAT-directed agents or clinical trials in refractory disease
Escalate immunosuppression for disease unresponsive to first-line treatment
